content: Substance use treatments such as methadone maintenance therapy (MMT) and buprenorphine maintenance therapy, combined with counseling, were recommended as preferred interventions. However, funding for naltrexone provision was discontinued after the conclusion of the study. In the United States, research by Sack et al. (2012) demonstrated that prison-based therapeutic treatments for women effectively reduced drug use, criminal activity, and trauma exposure while improving mental health and delaying re-incarceration. Similarly, Springer et al. (2010) found that buprenorphine induction and stabilization were effective, acceptable, and well-tolerated for preventing opiate relapse in HIV-infected prisoners post-release. This approach also maintained favorable HIV outcomes and potentially reduced HIV-associated morbidity and mortality. In Malaysia, Wickersham et al. (2013) implemented a standardized methadone initiation protocol starting four months before release. Methadone doses began at 5 mg daily, increasing weekly by 5 mg until reaching 80 mg/day or satisfying cravings. Participants were followed for 12 months post-release at MMT clinics within 25 kilometers of the prison. Higher methadone doses at release correlated with better retention in MMT programs after reintegration into the community. In India, a 2013 UNODC study reported a 98% retention rate for opioid substitution therapy (OST) clients in prison settings. The study observed significant reductions in drug dependence severity, cravings, withdrawal symptoms, and high-risk behaviors such as injecting drug use, needle sharing, and unsafe sexual practices. Prison authorities also noted improvements in inmates' health and hygiene. Challenges included unpredictable prisoner stays, lack of linkage to community programs upon release, and frequent staff turnover. In the United States, Freudenberg et al. (2010) evaluated an intensive 30-hour jail/community-based intervention compared to a single jail-based discharge planning session. Participants referred to community-based organization (CBO) services or assigned to the REAL MEN program showed significantly reduced odds of substance dependence one year post-release. HIV/AIDS education programs in prisons have shown promise in improving inmates' knowledge about HIV/AIDS. Studies across various countries, including lowand middle-income nations, highlight the need for well-designed educational initiatives. While knowledge alone is insufficient, it is a critical precursor to protective behaviors. Peer-led education programs have been particularly effective in reducing stigma and increasing awareness of HIV transmission. Factors influencing program success include comprehensiveness, population-specific tailoring, literacy appropriateness, peer involvement, and preand post-test counseling. In South Africa, Sifunda et al. (2008) conducted a six-week intervention led by trained peer educators, covering topics such as HIV/AIDS, STIs, nutrition, TB prevention, substance abuse, and life skills. Long-term results indicated improved safer sex practices and sexual negotiation skills. In the United States, Derlega et al. (2008) emphasized the importance of peer-based HIV education to reduce stigma and misinformation about HIV transmission. Fields et al. (2008) highlighted the critical role of comprehensive, peer-led education for program success. Ko et al. (2009) demonstrated that a brief TTM-based HIV education program effectively improved knowledge and skills among drug-dependent inmates, including safe injection practices and condom use. Martin et al. (2008) found that a DVD-based intervention group was less likely to engage in unprotected sex compared to standard intervention groups. Grinstead et al. (2008) reported that enhanced interventions (EI) were more effective than single-session interventions (SSI) in reducing sexual risk behaviors. Incentives were provided at weeks one and twelve. In Switzerland, Fluhmann et al. (2012) used a structured information exchange (StIE) model to present HIV and Hepatitis C information to prisoners at the start of their sentences. In the United States, Goldberg et al. (2009) found that education interventions with booster sessions sustained knowledge and prevention attitude improvements, particularly among males and females in the booster groups. Gurdin et al. (2008) implemented a short-term, intensive intervention consisting of four one-hour small-group sessions focused on health education, particularly HIV/AIDS. Participants reported more favorable attitudes toward condom use and increased likelihood of using condoms during intercourse compared to a comparison group. Hurd et al. (2010) evaluated a four-session adapted HIV prevention program and found positive changes across all study outcomes, with no significant differences between the fourand eight-session groups. Robertson et al. (2011) demonstrated that adolescent girls in an 18-session HIV risk reduction program acquired risk-reduction behaviors and improved condom application skills. Sexual violence in prisons remains a significant health threat, both physically and psychologically, including the risk of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. While some prison systems deny the problem, others have implemented measures to document incidents, prevent violence, train staff, and provide victim services, including post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Structural interventions, such as cameras and staff involvement in violence prevention, are essential. In the United States, La Vigne et al. (2011) piloted three interventions: electronic tracking of officer rounds, camera installation to reduce blind spots, and crisis intervention training for officers. Results varied, with fewer reported force incidents at one site and favorable impressions of training at another. In Australia, Yap et al. (2007) identified measures to reduce sexual assaults in prisons, including fewer prisoners per cell, in-cell toilets and showers, increased camera coverage, roaming guards, and housing inmates by risk level. Emphasis was placed on guards' duty of care obligations to protect vulnerable prisoners. HIV counseling and testing programs that are easily accessible upon prison entry and throughout incarceration increase testing uptake. Voluntary testing, confidentiality, and linkage to care are critical components. Mandatory testing and segregation are unethical, costly, and counterproductive. In Jamaica, Andrinopoulos et al. (2010) reported high acceptance rates for voluntary testing and assured confidentiality. In the United States, opt-out testing within 24 hours of incarceration increased acceptance rates among male and female prisoners.
